clue.text: A foreign correspondent

parts.note: surface reading: a journalist reporting from abroad for a newspaper
setter's reading: someone overseas you exchange personal letters with

explanation.surface: A newspaper's reporter posted abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correspondent' suggests the press, but anyone who writes letters is a correspondent, and a pen pal is often in another country.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen pal is someone, usually overseas, with whom you swap letters, so literally a correspondent from abroad.

clue.text: Fleece father's housemaster

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father, with the possessive s
HM is the abbreviation for housemaster

explanation.surface: A boarding-school housemaster who happens to be the speaker's dad.
explanation.walkthrough: A housemaster runs one of the boarding houses at a British public school; HM is its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Pashm is the fine woolly underfleece of Himalayan goats, the raw material of cashmere and pashmina shawls.

clue.text: Padded but not in the middle

definitions.text: Padded but not in the middle

parts.words: Padded but not in the middle
parts.note: surface reading: something stuffed with padding except at its centre
setter's reading: a cricketer wearing batting pads, waiting but not yet out in the middle of the pitch

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the waiting batsman sits padded up in the pavilion; 'the middle' is the cricketers' name for the pitch where batting happens.
explanation.definitionFit: The batter due to go in next sits wearing protective leg guards but has not yet walked out to the crease.

clue.text: Cheapskate first organised party machine to produce results with no pattern

definitions.text: machine to produce results with no pattern

indicators.note: first says the following words come before the cheapskate in the answer

parts.note: to run something is to organise it; ran is the past tense
a do is an informal party
a miser is a stingy person

explanation.surface: A tightwad throws a party first, then shows off a gadget producing random results.
explanation.definitionFit: A randomiser is a device that generates outcomes by chance, so its output follows no predictable sequence.

clue.text: For example, force copper coppers into small holders

parts.note: e.g. abbreviates 'for example'
g is the physics symbol for g-force, the force of gravity
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
coppers are pennies, and p is the abbreviation for a penny

explanation.surface: Police being forced into cramped cells, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: Coppers here are copper coins, British pennies, written p.
explanation.definitionFit: Egg cups are small cups that hold a boiled egg upright at the breakfast table.

clue.text: Data, mostly taking in Great Britain, concerning unnamed missile

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all of the word, so its final letter is dropped
taking means holding inside, so the shortened word wraps around what follows

parts.note: the word with its last letter cut
taken as written
GB is the abbreviation for Great Britain

explanation.surface: A report on British data about a missile whose name is withheld.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concerning' looks like part of the wordplay but only links it to the definition; 'unnamed' fits because a dingbat is also a thingummy.
explanation.definitionFit: Dingbat is an informal word for a thingummy, and in American slang an object such as a stone that is thrown.

clue.text: Five notes joined together

wordplay.note: five musical notes: A, D, D, E and D

explanation.surface: A musician strings five notes into a phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: The notes of the scale run A to G, so a word made only of those letters can be spelt in notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that have been added have been combined or attached to one another, put into one sum.

clue.text: A-class grass

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the code word used for the letter A in radio spelling
second meaning: esparto, a tough grass used for paper and rope

explanation.surface: Top-quality grass.
explanation.walkthrough: Alfa is how radio operators say A, so it stands in the A class; it is also another name for esparto.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfa is the NATO phonetic name for the first letter and also a North African grass gathered for paper-making.

clue.text: Very important show trial

parts.note: surface reading: a high-profile political trial staged for public effect
setter's reading: a trial run of a theatrical show, an important final one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Show trial' suggests a rigged court case; read as two words it is a test performance of a play.
explanation.definitionFit: The final full run-through of a play in costume before opening night is its most important practice performance.

clue.text: Make a timely impression

parts.note: surface reading: to arrive and impress people at just the right moment
setter's reading: an inked mark that records the day, pressed onto paper

explanation.walkthrough: An impression is also a printed mark; one that records the time is made with a rubber stamp.
explanation.definitionFit: To date-stamp a document is to press an inked mark onto it showing the day it was received.

clue.text: Six Scots talking about an old language

parts.note: sax is the Scots form of the number six
on means about, as in a talk on a subject

explanation.surface: Six Scotsmen chatting about an ancient tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Saxon is the Germanic language of the early Saxons, an ancestor of Old English.

clue.text: Show respect for man nursing dreadful clue about France

indicators.note: nursing means cradling inside, so the man holds the rest

parts.note: a gent is a man

indicators.note: something dreadful is a mess, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, to be mixed
F is the international code for France

explanation.surface: A man hugging a bad crossword clue about France to show his respect.
explanation.definitionFit: To genuflect is to bend the knee in worship or deference, a gesture of reverence.

clue.text: Silly talk of she-elephant having a nasty smell

indicators.note: having means holding within, so the she-elephant contains the smell

parts.note: mum, a mother, is a she
Jumbo is the classic name for an elephant
BO is body odour

explanation.surface: Gossip about a smelly cow elephant.
explanation.definitionFit: Mumbo-jumbo is meaningless or pretentious gibberish, nonsense words dressed up as meaning.

clue.text: Miss newfangled fads

indicators.note: newfangled means freshly reinvented, so the letters take a new form

parts.note: taken as written, to be mixed

explanation.surface: Someone skipping the latest trends.
explanation.definitionFit: Isms are distinctive doctrines or movements, often passing ones, like fashionable crazes.

clue.text: Zealous advocate may otherwise avenge record

indicators.note: otherwise means arranged differently, so the letters are put in another order

parts.note: taken as written, to be mixed
a list is a record

explanation.surface: A passionate campaigner might instead take revenge for some record.
explanation.definitionFit: An evangelist is an enthusiastic promoter of a cause, like a preacher spreading the gospel.

clue.text: A step in kinky underwear

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the letters are bent out of order

parts.note: taken as written, to be mixed

explanation.surface: Stepping into some racy lingerie.
explanation.definitionFit: Panties are short knickers, a woman's or girl's undergarment for the lower body.

clue.text: Polytechnic type almost in charge of many subdivisions

indicators.note: almost means nearly all, so the final letter is lost

parts.note: poly is the short form of polytechnic
the word with its last letter cut
i/c is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A sort of polytechnic that runs many departments.
explanation.walkthrough: Polytechnics were British colleges of higher education, called polys for short.
explanation.definitionFit: In biology polytypic describes a species that contains several subspecies or varieties.

clue.text: Get tax back and earn, we hear, a holiday place in Greece

indicators.note: back means turned round, so the tax word reads right to left

parts.note: VAT is value added tax

indicators.note: we hear points to the sound of earn, not its spelling

parts.note: an ern, or erne, is a sea eagle, said exactly like the clue word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Claim a tax refund and earn money in a Greek resort.
explanation.definitionFit: A taverna is a small Greek restaurant or inn, a fixture of holidays in Greece.

clue.text: See 7
Backed-up river's got nothing and produces yellow oil

indicators.note: backed-up means moved backwards, so everything that follows reads in reverse

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Britain, with the possessive s
nil means nothing

explanation.surface: A dammed river with no water left turns out yellow oil.
explanation.definitionFit: Linseed, the seed of flax, is pressed to give linseed oil, a yellowish oil used in paints and varnish.

clue.text: Portend new equipment for catching fish

indicators.note: new means remade, so these letters form a fresh word

parts.note: taken as written, to be mixed

explanation.surface: An omen of fresh fishing gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A drop-net is a net lowered into water and pulled up to trap fish or crabs.

clue.text: Fighting caused by drink at university

parts.note: punch is a mixed drink
up means in residence at university, as in up at Oxford

explanation.surface: A student brawl fuelled by alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: A punch-up is British slang for a fist fight.
explanation.definitionFit: A punch-up is a brawl, a bout of fighting with fists.

clue.text: Joke I made about "Punch" in another language

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the joke and I go round the punch

parts.note: a pun is a play on words
taken as written
a jab is a quick punch

explanation.surface: Someone translating a gag about the satirical magazine Punch.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch was a long-running British humour magazine; its quotation marks are part of the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Punjabi is the language of the Punjab region of India and Pakistan.

clue.text: Bound, they say, to ebb and flow

indicators.note: they say means as spoken, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

parts.note: bound means tied up

explanation.surface: Something certain to rise and fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' looks like 'certain to'; here bound means tied, a sound for the sea's movement.
explanation.definitionFit: The tide is the twice-daily rise and fall of the sea, its regular ebbing and flowing.

clue.text: A bunch of flowers

parts.note: surface reading: a bouquet of blooms
setter's reading: things that flow, rivers, splitting into many channels at a river mouth

explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords a flower is often something that flows, a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A river's mouth that fans out into many branching channels is a cluster of watercourses, named after the Greek letter's shape.

clue.text: Perform on flat surface and perform in the opposite direction

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the performing comes after the surface in the across answer

parts.note: a counter is a flat worktop
to act is to perform

explanation.surface: Instructions to dance on a tabletop and then do it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To counteract is to work against something, acting with opposite force to neutralise it.

clue.text: God beat around it

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the beating word encloses it

parts.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
taken as written

explanation.surface: A deity thrashing something.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titans were the giant elder gods of Greek mythology, overthrown by Zeus and the Olympians.

clue.text: Auntie's own protection against flooding?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Greg ..., then Director-General of the BBC, known as Auntie
second meaning: an embankment holding back water

explanation.surface: An aunt's personal flood barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: Auntie is the British nickname for the BBC, whose head when this was set was Greg Dyke.
explanation.definitionFit: A dyke is a bank built to keep the sea or a river from flooding land, and Greg Dyke ran the BBC.

clue.text: Two girls meet an optimist

parts.note: Polly is a girl's name
Anna is another girl's name

explanation.surface: Two young women are introduced to a cheerful person.
explanation.definitionFit: Pollyanna, heroine of a children's novel, gave her name to anyone relentlessly cheerful and hopeful.

clue.text: Tie poles into small diagram

indicators.note: into means made into something new, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written, to be mixed
north and south are the two poles

explanation.surface: Lashing stakes together into a little sketch.
explanation.walkthrough: Put the poles inside a rotated tie (IET) and you also get there; either way the letters must move.
explanation.definitionFit: An inset is a small map or picture set within a larger one, often showing detail.

clue.text: Raise a kind of fly

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a machine for lifting loads, or to lift
second meaning: the long-legged insect called a ... fly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise a fly' sounds like hoisting a flag or tent flap; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A crane hoists heavy objects aloft, and the daddy-long-legs insect is called a crane fly.

clue.text: Three-legged competition

parts.note: surface reading: a three-legged race, with partners' legs tied together
setter's reading: an endurance event split into three stages of swimming, cycling and running

explanation.walkthrough: A leg is also a stage of a race, so three legs means three stages.
explanation.definitionFit: The event combines swimming, cycling and running in succession, three stages in one endurance race.
